notice: Specification and acceptance contract only. Nothing here is approved, released or shown to work. No production lesson, ledger event, learner record, grade or mastery value is changed by this file. All defects are recorded by the specification author and require independent confirmation by a qualified reviewer.

basis.factoryCompatibility: Assessment entries map 1:1 onto Content Factory V2 unitBlueprintSchema.assessmentPlan (timing, scaffold, context REHEARSED|NEW, scoring KEYED|ANALYTIC_RUBRIC) and onto the pilot spec format liberialearn-modernization-spec/1.0.0.

selection.method: The author read the full learner text of 13 high-exposure eligible lessons (all with scheduled work or learner history) and selected on: (1) a factual, mathematical or scientific error confirmed by reading or recomputation; (2) current assignment and learner history; (3) foundational status; (4) subject coverage (Math 3, Literacy/English 2, Science 2, Civics 3); (5) grade-band coverage (G2, G5, G7). Lessons on governance hold (Track D) and the 6 lessons already awaiting review were excluded.
selection.gradeSkewNote: 7 of 10 are Grade 7 because the catalogue (481 of 1,105 lessons in G7-9) and its learner history are concentrated there. G1 civics and G6 math/literacy already have pilot candidates.
selection.classConcentrationNote: Four lessons come from the same wk_mca7a weekly series, each scheduled in exactly one class at one school. The inventory holds counts only, so whether this is the same class must be verified before one coordinated correction notice is planned.

rules: Mastery evidence counts only if collected END_OF_LESSON or DELAYED at scaffold NONE, with hints, worked examples, AI help and answer feedback withheld, and assistance recorded (LM-ASM-2).
Every objective is assessed at the end of the lesson, and every objective has a delayed retrieval item at least 7 days later.
Selected response is at most 60% of end-of-lesson mastery evidence (50% where original writing is central). It is used for misconception diagnosis, never as the only reasoning evidence.
Every distractor maps to a catalogued misconception with corrective feedback.
The transfer item uses a context, representation or genre the lesson did not rehearse.
Answer keys live only in the protected teacher/reviewer projection.
Every interactive element has an objective-preserving offline or text fallback.
Completion, time on task, and exposure are delivery evidence, never learning evidence.

verificationValues.MECHANICAL_AUDIT_CONFIRMED: Also reported by the committed mechanical audit at this revision.

lessons.legacyTitle: Exploring the Counties and Capitals of Liberia
lessons.subject: CIVICS
lessons.selectionNote: Learners are drilled to memorise a wrong capital: every worked example, guided problem and printed answer gives Ganta as Nimba's capital. 13 learners have progress on it, and the class has it on its schedule.

defects.legacy: Nimba County ... The capital city, Ganta
defects.correction: The capital of Nimba County is Sanniquellie. Ganta is Nimba's largest commercial town. Every answer key, worked example and error-analysis item that pairs Nimba with Ganta must change.

defects.legacy: Montserrado - Monrovia
defects.correction: Monrovia is the national capital. Standard references give Bensonville as the seat of Montserrado County. The reviewer confirms this against a current Ministry of Internal Affairs / LISGIS source, and the lesson then teaches national capital and county capital as separate ideas.

defects.legacy: For Maryland County, situate it adjacent to Sinoe
defects.correction: Grand Kru lies between Sinoe and Maryland. Maryland borders Grand Kru, River Gee and Côte d'Ivoire (along the Cavalla River).

defects.legacy: Identify and name all 15 counties
defects.correction: Only 10 counties are taught. Gbarpolu (Bopolu), Grand Gedeh (Zwedru), Grand Kru (Barclayville), River Cess (Cestos City) and River Gee (Fish Town) never appear.

defects.legacy: Each county in Liberia corresponds uniquely to a capital city that governs it
defects.correction: A capital does not govern its county. Liberia is a unitary state, and county administration is led by a superintendent whom the President appoints. Unsourced economic claims (Nimba 'contributing significantly to the country's GDP', 'tourism in Bong') must be sourced or removed.

defects.legacy: Answer: The capital of Lofa County is Voinjama.
defects.correction: Every independent item prints its answer, and the exit ticket has no key. A geography objective is never assessed with a map.

objectives.statement: Locate each of Liberia's 15 counties on an outline map and name its capital.

Explain the difference between a county capital (the seat of county administration) and a county's largest or best-known town, and between the national capital and a county capital, using Nimba (Sanniquellie/Ganta) and Montserrado as examples.
Use a county map to reason about location: name the counties crossed, and the capitals passed, on a route between two county capitals, and justify the answer from the map.

prerequisites.fallbackRoute: A 4-minute directions mini-scene (sun rises in the east; the map key) before the county map.

prerequisites.fallbackRoute: A nested-boxes visual: Liberia → county → district → town, using the learner's own county.

Fading: labelled map → partially labelled map → blank map

The Mano River border with Sierra Leone and the Cavalla River border with Côte d'Ivoire

lessons.legacyTitle: The Founding of Liberia: Historical Context and Significance
lessons.subject: CIVICS
lessons.selectionNote: Core national history is taught with wrong facts about founders and places. All of its practice is Liberian-dollar subtraction, so none of the three history objectives is practised or assessed.

defects.legacy: Joseph Jenkins Roberts, a freed slave who became one of the first governors
defects.correction: Joseph Jenkins Roberts was born free in Norfolk, Virginia (1809) and emigrated in 1829. He became the Commonwealth's first Black governor (1841) and Liberia's first President (1848).

defects.legacy: Cuffe worked with the ACS ... and he helped to recruit settlers for the new colony
defects.correction: Paul Cuffe died in 1817. His 1815–16 voyage took 38 emigrants to Sierra Leone. He corresponded with ACS founders, but he did not recruit settlers for Liberia, which began in 1822.

defects.legacy: arrived on the shores of the St. Paul River in the early 19th century; In 1822, the ACS established the colony of Liberia, which was named after ...
defects.correction: The first ACS emigrants (the Elizabeth, 1820) landed at Sherbro Island in present-day Sierra Leone. The settlement at Cape Mesurado (Providence Island) began in 1822, and the name 'Liberia' was adopted in 1824.

defects.legacy: The river that runs through the city of Monrovia is the St. Paul River.
defects.correction: Monrovia was founded on Cape Mesurado at the mouth of the Mesurado River. The St. Paul River forms the northern edge of Greater Monrovia (Bushrod Island). The key must not teach the St. Paul as the river running through the city; the reviewer confirms the wording.

defects.legacy: If Pewee ... traveled to Liberia in 1822 with 50 LD in his pocket ...
defects.correction: Every worked example and practice item is money subtraction and is unrelated to the history objectives. Liberian-dollar amounts in 1822–1825 are also anachronistic: the reviewer confirms that a Liberian currency was not issued before independence. Replace all of it with historical-thinking tasks.

defects.legacy: conflict with local tribes; Civilization: the idea that Western culture is superior
defects.correction: Indigenous peoples appear only as an obstacle; Dei, Bassa, Vai and other communities already living on the coast need their own perspective, with sources. 'Civilization' is mis-defined as an ideology: teach the ACS 'civilising mission' as the historical ideology and keep the ordinary meaning of the word separate.

defects.legacy: the country's struggle for independence and its experiences during the colonial era
defects.correction: Liberia declared independence on 26 July 1847 and was not colonised by a European power. Present the ACS-administered settlement period accurately.

objectives.statement: Place the key events of Liberia's founding (ACS 1816; Sherbro 1820; Cape Mesurado 1822; the name Liberia 1824; independence 26 July 1847) in order on a timeline and describe each in one sentence.

Explain the different motives and experiences of three groups (ACS supporters, Black American emigrants, and the Indigenous communities already living on the coast), using evidence from at least two short sources.
Evaluate a historical claim about the founding (e.g. 'Liberia was an American colony') by weighing evidence for and against it.

prerequisites.statement: Reads a timeline (earlier/later; decades).
prerequisites.diagnostic: Which came first, 1822 or 1847? How many years apart are they?
prerequisites.fallbackRoute: A timeline warm-up using the learner's own school years.

prerequisites.statement: Knows the difference between a fact and an opinion.
prerequisites.diagnostic: Two-item sort: 'The ACS was founded in 1816' / 'The settlers were brave'.
prerequisites.fallbackRoute: A fact/opinion sorting scene with feedback.

misconceptions.feedback: The ACS was a private society. The US government did not rule the settlement, and it recognised Liberia only in 1862.

misconceptions.feedback: Many emigrants, Roberts among them, were born free.

misconceptions.feedback: Dei, Bassa, Vai and other peoples already lived and traded on this coast.

misconceptions.description: Confusing 1822 (settlement) with 1847 (independence).
misconceptions.feedback: 1822: the settlement begins. 1847: the Republic is declared.

lessons.legacyTitle: Understanding Democracy and Representation in Liberia
lessons.subject: CIVICS
lessons.selectionNote: The most-scheduled lesson in the shortlist (55 scheduled-work rows across 2 classes). It implies that Liberia elects its legislature by proportional representation, and its own seat allocation adds up to 11 of 10 seats.

defects.legacy: Elections and proportional representation are mechanisms that ensure diverse and fair governance ... allowing minority voices from areas like rural Nimba
defects.correction: Liberia's House of Representatives has 73 members, each elected from a single-member electoral district by plurality. The Senate has two senators per county (30), equal for every county regardless of population. Proportional allocation may appear only as a labelled comparison model, never as Liberia's system.

defects.legacy: Community A ... ~ 3; B ~ 2; C ~ 1; D ~ 1; E ~ 4 (10 representatives total)
defects.correction: The rounded allocation totals 3+2+1+1+4 = 11 seats, not 10. The mechanical auditor cannot detect this. Any apportionment example must state its method (e.g. largest remainder) and sum correctly.

defects.where: delivery.body §7 step 1 vs 'What Do You Notice'
defects.legacy: Regardless of the differences in population size, each community's voice should resonate with equal significance ... This method illustrates equality ... through proportional representation
defects.correction: This contradicts itself: equal representation per unit (like the Senate) and population-proportional representation (like the House principle) are different ideas. Teach the contrast explicitly.

defects.legacy: Gbanyan, our Superintendent ... This is representation
defects.correction: County superintendents are appointed by the President, not elected. Teach elected versus appointed offices.

defects.legacy: "Legis-late" – laws ... take time ("late"); "stituency" can refer to state; Each LD$ possesses intrinsic value
defects.correction: The etymologies are false: legislative comes from Latin lex/legis 'law' + latio 'proposing'. Paper currency has no intrinsic value; remove the analogy.

defects.legacy: Identify the roles of key representatives such as the President, Senators, and House of Representatives members
defects.correction: Roles, terms of office (President 6 years; Senators 9; Representatives 6, per the 1986 Constitution as reviewer-confirmed) and the three branches are not taught. Worked examples are arithmetic apportionment, not civics.

defects.legacy: Flesch-Kincaid grade 13.9; 6 sections over 300 words
defects.correction: Rewrite to the Grade 7 band, one idea per scene.

objectives.statement: Describe Liberia's three branches of government and who is elected to each, and how: the President nationally, two senators per county, and one representative per electoral district.
Explain representation and accountability, and distinguish elected offices from appointed ones (e.g. superintendent, cabinet minister) using Liberian examples.
Compare equal representation per county (Senate) with population-based representation (House), and argue one advantage and one disadvantage of each, with reasons.

lessons.legacyTitle: Understanding States of Matter Through Real-Life Examples
lessons.subject: SCIENCE
lessons.selectionNote: The lesson teaches physically impossible results: ice in juice warms the mixture to 80 °C, and boiling water drops to −71.5 °C and 'boils off'. It does this with senior-secondary calorimetry while the Grade 7 particle model goes untaught.

defects.legacy: The final temperature of the mixture is approximately 80.0°C.
defects.correction: Cooling 300 g of juice to 0 °C releases at most 31,350 J, less than the 33,400 J needed to melt 100 g of ice. So about 93.9 g melts, about 6.1 g of ice remains, and the mixture stays at 0 °C. A mixture can never end hotter than its hottest part.
8,360 + 133,600 = 141,960. Cooling the water to 0 °C releases 83,600 J. After 8,360 J warms the ice, 75,240 J melts about 225 g, leaving about 175 g of ice at 0 °C. Nothing boils off.

defects.legacy: Q = m * L_f = 500 g * 334 = 167,000 J; Likely between 11-15°C final; they will meet at 0-1°C
defects.correction: Freezing 500 g of water from 30 °C needs 62,700 J (cooling) + 167,000 J = 229,700 J removed. 250 g of ice at −5 °C in 300 g of water at 20 °C ends at 0 °C with about 67 g melted, not 11–15 °C. Two samples of ice alone end below 0 °C (−3.75 °C), with no liquid. The keys are vague ('likely', 'around') or wrong.

defects.legacy: Specific heat of water = 4.18 J/g·°C; Latent heat of fusion for ice = 334 J/g
defects.correction: Quantitative latent-heat calorimetry is senior-secondary physics. Grade 7 needs the particle model, the changes of state and the energy direction. Calculation may appear only as an optional, labelled extension.

defects.legacy: the solid ice melts, but it also creates a reaction; This process is called evaporation [boiling]; Palm oil on a hot stove will eventually evaporate
defects.correction: Melting is a physical change, not a reaction; fizzing comes from dissolved gas. Boiling and evaporation are different processes. Cooking oil smokes and breaks down rather than simply evaporating, so it is a poor example.

defects.legacy: What was the most surprising fact you learned
defects.correction: The exit ticket does not assess any objective and has no key.

objectives.statement: Use the particle model to describe and compare solids, liquids and gases (arrangement, movement, shape and volume), with Liberian examples.
Explain melting, freezing, evaporation, boiling and condensation as energy gained or lost by particles, and distinguish evaporation from boiling.
Predict and explain, with evidence, what happens to temperature when ice melts in a drink (it stays at about 0 °C while ice remains), and recognise changes of state as reversible physical changes.

prerequisites.statement: Reads a thermometer in °C.
prerequisites.diagnostic: Read two thermometer pictures (25 °C and 0 °C).
prerequisites.fallbackRoute: A thermometer-reading mini-scene.

prerequisites.statement: Knows that all matter is made of tiny particles.
prerequisites.diagnostic: True/false: 'Air is made of nothing.'
prerequisites.fallbackRoute: A particles-in-air demonstration scene (the smell of cooking spreads across the room).

progression: Diagnose thermometer reading and the particle idea

liberianContexts: A cold water bottle 'sweating' in Monrovia's humid air (condensation)
Fish and cassava drying in the sun (evaporation)
Palm oil thickening on a cool morning and flowing when warmed (reviewer to confirm the description)

visualAndInteractive.requirement: A particle simulation with a heat slider showing arrangement and motion in each state, with a text description of every state.
visualAndInteractive.offlineFallback: A printed three-panel particle diagram and a role-play (learners as particles).

visualAndInteractive.requirement: A heating curve for water with labelled plateaus, built step by step.

visualAndInteractive.offlineFallback: A recorded data table for classes without ice or a thermometer.

misconceptions.description: The bubbles in boiling water are air.
misconceptions.feedback: They are water vapour forming inside the liquid.

misconceptions.description: The temperature keeps rising while ice melts, or a mixture can get hotter than its hottest part.
misconceptions.feedback: While ice is melting, the energy goes into changing state and the temperature stays near 0 °C.

misconceptions.description: Water on a cold bottle leaks through the plastic.
misconceptions.feedback: Water vapour from the air condenses on the cold surface.

misconceptions.description: Evaporation only happens at 100 °C.
misconceptions.feedback: Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

misconceptions.description: The particles themselves expand or melt.
misconceptions.feedback: The particles stay the same; their spacing and motion change.

misconceptions.description: Melting is a chemical reaction.
misconceptions.feedback: No new substance forms, and the change reverses.

items: Name the change of state in three scenes

lessons.selectionNote: 51 learning events across 2 classes, plus 10 video supplements attached. The science has been replaced with multiplication on invented 'grams of glucose per plant per day' rates.

defects.legacy: each plant can produce 5 grams of glucose each day

defects.legacy: Boima will collect 350 grams of glucose; Photosynthesis is the process by which plants convert light into energy
defects.correction: Glucose is not collected: the plant uses it for respiration and growth or stores it (in cassava, as starch in the roots). Light energy is changed into chemical energy; energy is not made from nothing.

defects.legacy: Is it just from the soil?
defects.correction: The central Grade 5 misconception, that plants get their food from the soil, is raised and never addressed.

defects.legacy: This reaction makes the water absorbed by the roots split into oxygen and hydrogen ... including its stages
defects.correction: Water splitting and 'stages' are beyond Grade 5 (Flesch-Kincaid 11.5). Keep the inputs, the outputs and the role of light.

defects.legacy: 8 palm oil plants
defects.correction: The plant is the oil palm; palm oil is its product. The mnemonic 'stomata sounds like stomach' reinforces the idea that plants eat, so remove it.

defects.legacy: **Answer**: **150 grams**
defects.correction: Answers are printed beside the practice items, and the exit ticket has no key.

lessons.legacyTitle: Calculating Area and Perimeter of Polygons for Real-World Applications
lessons.subject: MATH
lessons.selectionNote: The most-used math lesson: 42 scheduled-work rows, 44 learning events and 1 assignment. It gives two different areas for the same field, and its assessment item ends unsolved with a chatbot prompt.

defects.legacy: Total area of all rows: 10 × 450 = 4500 ... Verify again if the distribution was miscalculated
defects.correction: 90 × 45 = 4,050 m², as §7 shows. The 'alternative method' produces 4,500 m², and the text leaves the contradiction unresolved.

defects.legacy: explore outside resources for real applications ... **Tell me more about whether assumptions hold.**
defects.correction: The rhombus item is left unsolved, with generator residue. With side 6 m and one diagonal 8 m, the other diagonal is 2√20 ≈ 8.94 m, the area ≈ 35.8 m² and the perimeter 24 m. Either solve it within Grade 7 scope or replace it.

defects.legacy: the height (distance from the center to a vertex) is 2.6 meters
defects.correction: 2.6 m is the apothem (centre to the midpoint of a side). For a regular hexagon with side 3 m, the centre-to-vertex distance is 3 m.

defects.legacy: the area of one of Fatu's square tiles is 16 square meters, and the perimeter is also 16 meters
defects.correction: This treats 16 m² and 16 m as comparable, which reinforces the area/perimeter confusion, and a 4 m tile is unrealistic. Use 30 cm or 40 cm tiles, and contrast units explicitly.

defects.legacy: studentPrompt: 20 × 10 ...; answerKey: 20 + 14 = 34 ... 280 square meters
defects.correction: The prompt and its key describe different problems. Every key must match its prompt exactly.

defects.legacy: Explain the significance of choosing the appropriate polygon shape for maximizing area while minimizing the perimeter
defects.correction: Never taught: there is no fixed-perimeter comparison. The trapezoid problem (GP3) does not say which sides are parallel, so its area is ill-posed.

defects.legacy: Area of one triangle = 1200 m² / 2 = 600 square meters
defects.correction: A practice answer leaked into the summary.

lessons.legacyTitle: Understanding and Representing Fractions in Real-Life Contexts
lessons.subject: MATH
lessons.selectionNote: Used in 2 schools (12 progress records and 19 learning events). It mis-defines a fraction, marks a correct method as an error, and never teaches its compare objective, the same pattern the G6 decimals pilot found.

defects.legacy: Fraction: A numerical quantity that is not a whole number
defects.correction: Fractions can equal whole numbers (4/4 = 1; 12/4 = 3, both in this lesson) and can be greater than 1. Define a fraction as a number that names equal parts of a whole, or a point on the number line.

defects.legacy: Incorrect Answer: (3/4)/(1/4) = 3/1 = 3 ... they omit the process of flipping the divisor
defects.correction: Counting how many quarters are in three quarters is a correct method with a correct answer. Labelling it an error penalises understanding. Division of fractions is also outside the stated objectives.

defects.legacy: 2/1 ÷ 2 = 2/2 = 1 kg ... And he keeps the other kg: 2/2 = 1/1
defects.correction: This conflates a fraction of the bag with kilograms. Half of the bag is 1/2 of 2 kg = 1 kg. Always name the whole the fraction refers to.

defects.legacy: Compare and simplify fractions.
defects.correction: Comparison is never taught. The lesson also jumps to unlike denominators and division without teaching equivalence first.

defects.legacy: 1/2 a liter of palm oil ... a bag of palm oil that weighs 3 kilograms ... 1/4 kilogram packets
defects.correction: Palm oil switches between litres and kilograms. Use one measure, consistently and realistically.

objectives.statement: Represent fractions, including fractions equal to or greater than 1, on area models and a number line, naming the whole each fraction refers to.

lessons.legacyTitle: Understanding Vocabulary in Context Through West African Stories
lessons.subject: ENGLISH
lessons.selectionNote: The only English lesson with scheduled work (27 rows). It promises West African texts but supplies none: its 'West African' tales have tigers, foxes and cobblestone streets. Authoring word-count instructions such as '(600+ words)' appear in learner headings.

defects.legacy: an audacious tiger ... The cunning fox ... Liberian folktale; a 'quaint' village ... cobblestone streets
defects.correction: Tigers are not native to Africa, and foxes are not animals of Liberia's forests. 'Cobblestone streets' is European imagery. Use authentic or carefully authored West African material, such as Liberian Spider trickster tales, and attribute Anansi to Akan (Ghanaian) tradition.

defects.legacy: ## 1. Hook — The Real-World Challenge (300+ words); ## 7. Worked Example 1 — Standard Method (600+ words)
defects.correction: Generator length instructions are visible to learners. The mechanical audit does not catch this; add a check.

defects.legacy: With fervor akin to a hunted deer
defects.correction: A hunted deer suggests fear, not fervour, so the example contradicts the target meaning. The false mnemonic 'inferring — in-fuse' must also go.

defects.legacy: Flesch-Kincaid grade 13.5; largest section 1671 words
defects.correction: Rewrite to the Grade 7 band, one idea per scene. Choose high-utility Tier 2 target words, not low-utility ones like 'ballyhoo'.

objectives.statement: Use four kinds of context clue (definition or restatement, synonym, contrast, example) to infer the meaning of unfamiliar Tier 2 words in a West African passage.
Check an inferred meaning by substituting it into the sentence and confirming it with a dictionary or glossary.
Explain how a word's connotation shapes the meaning or tone of a passage, with evidence.

prerequisites.statement: Identifies nouns, verbs and adjectives in a sentence.
prerequisites.diagnostic: Two quick part-of-speech items.
prerequisites.fallbackRoute: A parts-of-speech refresher scene.

prerequisites.statement: Uses a dictionary or glossary entry.
prerequisites.diagnostic: Find the meaning in a glossary snippet.
prerequisites.fallbackRoute: A glossary-reading scene.

progression: Diagnose parts of speech and glossary use
Why context matters (one word, two meanings)
Clue types one at a time, each with signal words
liberianContexts: A Liberian Spider trickster tale (a public-domain or licensed version, or one authored and reviewed for cultural accuracy)
An excerpt by a West African author, subject to the licensing decision
A notice-board text from a Liberian school (authored and labelled)

visualAndInteractive.requirement: A clue-finder: tap the clue words in a passage and choose the clue type, with feedback naming the signal word.
visualAndInteractive.offlineFallback: A printed passage; learners underline clue words and label the type.

visualAndInteractive.requirement: A substitution checker: type an inferred meaning and the sentence is reread with it, and the learner judges the fit.
visualAndInteractive.offlineFallback: A partner read-aloud check.

guidedPractice: One clue type per sentence, with signal words highlighted
A short passage with highlighting removed
A connotation pair with a hint
Glossary confirmation

endOfLesson.task: Infer the meanings of four words in a new 150-word passage and name the clue type for each.
Show the substitution check for one word and say whether the inferred meaning fits.
Write 3–4 sentences explaining how replacing one word in the passage with a near-synonym changes its tone.
Four items whose distractors are mapped to M1–M5.

misconceptions.description: Any nearby word defines the target.
misconceptions.probe: A distractor taken from a non-clue word
misconceptions.feedback: Find the signal word that links the clue to the target.

misconceptions.description: One clue is enough, so there is no need to check.
misconceptions.feedback: Substitute the meaning and reread.

misconceptions.description: Context clues are guessing.
misconceptions.feedback: An inference must point to evidence in the text.

misconceptions.description: Ignoring contrast signals ('but', 'unlike') and inferring the opposite meaning.
misconceptions.feedback: 'But' signals the opposite of what came before.

misconceptions.description: Synonyms always have exactly the same meaning and tone.
misconceptions.feedback: 'Bold' and 'reckless' are close in meaning but differ in tone.

items: Two words in a new sentence, each with its clue type
A contrast clue
A connotation pair

transfer.task: A health notice (authored and labelled) with three unfamiliar words: infer each meaning and say which clue helped.

extension.task: Find a word in a Liberian newspaper or radio script whose meaning you inferred from context, and record the sentence and source.

teacherReview: Texts are authentically West African, or authored and reviewed for cultural accuracy, and licensing is recorded.
No authoring instructions or word-count markers remain in learner text.
Target words are high-utility Tier 2 words with a rationale.
Every example sentence actually supports the target meaning.

moeWaec.waec: LJHSCE English Language: vocabulary in context (evidence specificity LOW).
moeWaec.ceiling: The connotation writing task is mastery-level.

correctionNotice.reason: There are no exam-critical false facts, but teachers should be told about the misattributed folklore.

openDecisions.question: May excerpts from living West African authors be used?
openDecisions.authorRecommendation: Not until a licensing decision is made. Until then, use public-domain or LiberiaLearn-authored texts that a Liberian reviewer has checked.

alternates.legacyTitle: Understanding Food Chains and Biodiversity in Liberian Ecosystems
alternates.subject: SCIENCE
alternates.note: First alternate (science). 41 scheduled-work rows and 33 learning events. It teaches that energy flows in a cycle ('cyclical flow of energy and nutrients'), places toucans in Nimba (toucans are Neotropical; Liberia has hornbills), says cassava harvests depend on pollinators (cassava is grown from cuttings), and leaves its check-for-understanding answers blank.

alternates.legacyTitle: Making Smart Choices: Budgeting and Decision-Making at the Market
alternates.subject: MATH
alternates.note: Alternate (math). Dense arithmetic errors: 2 kg of rice + 3 kg of cassava costed as 90 LD (it is 105), 40×4 given as 120, '13 tons of rice', bottles counted as kilograms. Its objectives are speaking and listening skills mislabelled as Math. Low exposure: 1 learning event, no scheduled work.

alternates.subject: LITERACY
alternates.note: Alternate (literacy). Defines present tense as 'happening now' while every example is habitual, and never teaches irregular past forms. 7 learners in progress. It has a duplicate-title sibling (an elite variant) to resolve in the mapping plan.
